slides.title: A zone needs its full address
body: Overview › All zones: every zone, grouped by room.
Selected room: one room, chosen with its room chip.
slides.narration: Think of a block of flats. Flat two in one building is not flat two in the building next door. Zones work the same way. Remember from A one: a zone is a group of plants watered together. A room is a space with its own lights, and it holds one or more zones. Open the isolated demo, the practice copy that runs no equipment, and select Overview, the screen for checking rooms and zones. Its first tab, All zones, shows a card for every zone, grouped by room. The second tab, Selected room, shows one room at a time. Across the top, each room has a small button with its name, called a room chip. Select a chip, then select a zone card. That opens the zone page: one page about one zone. Zone two in Room A and Zone two in Room B are different addresses. Next, you check how fresh the information on that page is.

options.feedback: Right. The room chip sets the room; the zone number only means something inside that room.

options.text: The Room A chip, because it is listed first.
options.feedback: List order does not choose the room. Select the room you actually need: Room B.

slides.title: Check when each source last reported
body: Top bar: how long ago the Controller last reported.
Each probe keeps its own last report time.
slides.narration: Yesterday’s weather report cannot tell you if it is raining now. Every number on screen has an age too. Remember from C one: Home Assistant collects readings and switches equipment. Each named reading or control inside it is an entity, and each entity keeps the time of its own last report. Look at the top bar, the strip across the top of every page. Beside the room chips, it shows how long ago the Controller last reported for this room. That regular message from the Controller, saying it is running, is called a heartbeat. A probe has its own last report time. The Equipment screen, on its Probes tab, shows it for every probe. Here is an example. The top bar says the Controller reported one minute ago. The moisture probe last reported at nine in the morning, and it is now one in the afternoon. From nine to one is four hours, so that moisture reading is four hours old. Check each source’s own age before you trust its number. Next, read the reason the Controller gives.

check.prompt: Top bar: Controller reported 2 minutes ago. The VWC probe last reported at 06:00. It is now 11:00. How old is the VWC reading?

options.text: 2 minutes
options.feedback: That is the Controller’s heartbeat. The probe keeps its own report time: 06:00.

options.text: 5 hours
options.feedback: Right. From 06:00 to 11:00 is 5 hours. The fresh heartbeat does not refresh the probe.

options.text: It cannot be known.
options.feedback: It can. Subtract the probe’s last report time from the time now: 11 − 6 = 5 hours.

slides.title: Read the reason beside the state
body: Zone page: phase, last shot and Why / next action.
Why / next action: the reason now and what it waits for.
slides.narration: When a bus is late, the board at the stop usually says why. The zone page has the same kind of board. On the zone page, find three things. The phase, which you met in B two. The last shot. And the panel called Why slash next action. That panel gives the Controller’s reason for what it is doing now, and the condition it is waiting for next. Here is an example. The zone is in P two. The last shot was at nine twelve. The panel says it is waiting for moisture to fall to the re-water threshold of sixty percent. The probe reads sixty three percent. Sixty three minus sixty is three points still to dry, so no shot is due yet. That pause is the rule working as designed. The Controller’s records say what it decided; to see that water reached the plants, you look at the pots. Next, you put these pieces together in a worked example.

check.prompt: Zone in P2. Last shot 10:05. Why / next action: waiting for VWC to fall to 58%. Probe reads 61%. What do you conclude?

options.text: A fault: no shot has followed.
options.feedback: The panel explains the wait. 61 − 58 = 3 points still to dry before a shot is due.

options.text: Lower the re-water threshold so it waters now.
options.feedback: The rule is working. A normal wait needs no target change.

options.text: No shot is due yet; 3 points still to dry.
options.feedback: Right. 61 − 58 = 3. The Controller is waiting by its rule.

slides.title: Worked example: Training East, Zone 2
body: Training East chip pressed: Zone 2, P2, last shot 09:12.
Watering and Stop all act on the selected room only.
A shared pump stops for every room it feeds.
slides.narration: Now add the two controls in the top bar. In this fictional paper example, the Training East chip is pressed, so Training East is the selected room. Zone two is in P two. Its last shot was at nine twelve. Why slash next action says it is waiting for moisture to fall. Now look at the top bar. Watering is the room’s on and off permission for the Controller. When Watering is off, the Controller starts no shots in that room, rescue shots included. Stop all turns Watering off, then switches every pump and valve of that room off, and reads each one back. Both controls act on the selected room only, Training East. One more idea: a shared pump is one pump that feeds more than one room. If Training East shares its pump with Training West, Stop all also stops that pump, so Training West loses water too. The review box warns you about this. Read it before you confirm. Next, you meet a state the screen cannot confirm.

options.feedback: Its valves go off, but so does the shared pump. Training South loses water too.

options.text: North’s pumps and valves go off; South loses water from the shared pump.
options.feedback: Right. Stop all acts on the selected room, and shared equipment reaches further.

options.text: Every room on the site stops.
options.feedback: Stop all acts on the selected room. Only equipment that room shares reaches further.

slides.title: Your turn: finish an honest record
body: Room B, Zone 1: record pump state and report age as shown.
Unknown means the app cannot confirm the state.
Mapping: the link from a screen name to a real device.
slides.narration: A fuel gauge showing dashes instead of a number does not mean the tank is empty. It means the gauge cannot tell. The app does the same. When it cannot confirm a state, it shows the word unknown. For example, the top bar reads Watering unknown when that switch is missing or not answering in Home Assistant. Now practise in the demo. Select Room B, then Zone one. Find the pump state and its report age. Write them down exactly as displayed. If a state says unknown, write unknown. Writing off instead would claim something nobody confirmed. Then check the source, meaning the real device behind the display. The link between a name on screen and a real device is called a mapping. It is set up under Equipment, Setup. You check a mapping with the person who installed it, by reading the setup, rather than pressing buttons to see what moves. Next, find another zone on your own.

options.text: Pump: off.
options.feedback: Off is a confirmed state. Unknown means nobody confirmed it. Write what the screen shows.

options.text: Nothing, until it shows a real value.
options.feedback: Leaving it out hides a problem. Record unknown so someone checks the source.

options.text: Pump: unknown, with its report age.
options.feedback: Right. An honest record keeps the uncertainty visible.

slides.title: Find another zone independently
body: Record room, zone, phase, last shot, report ages, next action.
Settings & help › Settings › Display › Default view.
slides.narration: Now find a zone without the example, like finding a friend’s flat with only the address. Choose any other demo zone. Write six things: the room, the zone number, the phase, the last shot time, the report ages and the next action. Then choose where the app opens. Open Settings and help, then Settings, then Display, then Default view. The default view is the page this browser shows first when you open the app. For example, choose Selected room if you check one room every morning. This choice lives only in this browser. Another person’s phone keeps its own choice, and nothing about watering changes. A saved bookmark still opens the page it points to. Return to Overview and say the selected room’s name aloud before you read any card. That habit stops you reading one room’s numbers while thinking of another. The last slide checks what you remember.

slides.title: Recall the address and control scope
body: Top bar controls act on the selected room only.
To know water stopped, look at the outlets.
slides.narration: Close your notes and answer three questions aloud, the way a pilot repeats instructions back. First: which room do Watering and Stop all act on? The selected room, the one whose chip is pressed. Second: what does unknown tell you? That the app cannot confirm the state, so you record unknown and check the source. Third: after Stop all, how do you know the water really stopped? You look at the outlets and drippers. Off on the screen is a report from software. Remember from C one: the physical shutdown is the hand-operated way to cut water or power at the equipment itself. If water keeps flowing when it should not, use the physical shutdown first, then investigate. Tomorrow, repeat the navigation with a different demo address. Work on real equipment comes after your site’s responsible person has shown you around it. Next lesson, you change one target safely.

options.text: Trust the screen; off means stopped.
options.feedback: The dripper shows water still flowing. What you see at the outlet wins.

options.text: Press Stop all again and wait.
options.feedback: Repeating a software request delays the fix. Cut the water at the equipment first.

title: Change one target and see the curve move
summary: Change one target the safe way: read who owns it, draft, review, apply, read back, then restore.
outcomes: Read Target source and say who owns today’s targets.
Tell the saved reference, the draft and the recorded lines apart.
Draft, review and apply one allowed step on the Rescue floor, then read back and restore it.
Explain why the Rescue floor is a night alarm, not a nightly target.

slides.title: Begin by reading who owns the targets
body: Irrigation › Current day › Zone › Target source.
Armed schedule: a grow plan owns targets; edit in Calendar.
slides.narration: Before you edit a shared document, you check whether someone else is editing it. Targets work the same way. Remember from B two: a target is a comparison value the Controller’s rules use. Open Irrigation, then its first tab, Current day. Choose a zone from the Zone list. Under the tabs, read the line that starts Target source. It names who owns today’s targets. Manual room targets means you set them here. Automatic setpoints means the app can adjust some targets by itself. Setpoint is another word for target. Armed schedule means a grow plan owns them. A grow plan is a dated timetable of targets, which you build in the next lesson. When a plan owns the targets, this page shows them read only. You change them in Calendar, the planning screen. For practice, pick a demo room whose Target source is not armed schedule. Two owners writing the same target would undo each other’s work. Next, look at the chart beside the targets.

options.text: Calendar, because the grow plan owns the targets.

options.feedback: Setup holds substrate, sizing and safety limits, not daily targets.

slides.title: Tell the three lines apart
body: Saved reference: the target stored now.
Draft: your proposed change, not yet sent.
Solid dark lines: what the probes recorded.
slides.narration: A recipe card, your pencil notes on it, and the meal you actually cooked are three different things. The Current day chart shows three matching lines. Remember from B one: a dashed line is a planning reference and a solid line is measured. The saved reference shows the target values stored now. The draft shows a change you have proposed but not sent. As in B one, a draft is an unsaved proposal. Here it lives only in this browser until you apply it. The dark solid lines show what the zone’s probes recorded. Use the legend to match each name to its line. Here is an example. The saved re-water threshold sits at sixty percent. You drag the draft to sixty one. The draft line moves up one point. The saved line stays at sixty. The recorded moisture line does not move at all, because it is history. Mixing these up makes people think an edit changed the plants. Next, you learn what the setting you are about to edit actually does.

options.text: Only the draft line.

options.text: The draft and the recorded moisture line.
options.feedback: Recorded readings are history. An edit cannot change them.

options.text: The saved reference line.
options.feedback: The saved line moves only after Apply and a good readback.

slides.title: Learn what the setting means
body: Rescue floor: the P3 safety level for a rescue shot.
Read the ? help, unit and allowed step; note the start value.
slides.narration: A smoke alarm is not the temperature you set the heater to. It acts only when something goes wrong. Select the question mark beside a setting. This is the field help: a short note on what the setting does, when it acts and what it changes. For this exercise, find the P three setting labelled Rescue floor. You met it in B two, where growers also call it the emergency floor. The help calls it the overnight safety level of water content. In P three, the Controller gives a rescue shot each time moisture is below it. So it is a night alarm, not a level to aim for every night. Next, read its unit and its step. The unit is percent VWC. The step is the smallest change the setting accepts. We call it the allowed step. If the allowed step is one point, thirty can become thirty one, but not thirty point four. Write down the starting value before you touch anything. You need it to put things back. Next, you make the change.

visual.title: Learn what the setting means

check.prompt: A setting’s allowed step is 0.5 points. It reads 35%. Which value can you set next?

options.feedback: 0.2 is smaller than the step. Values move in multiples of 0.5.
1.3 is not a multiple of 0.5. Try 35.5 or 36.
Right. 35 + 0.5 = 35.5, one allowed step.

slides.title: Worked example: 30 becomes a 31 draft
body: Saved 30%, step 1 point: draft 30 + 1 = 31%.
Review changes lists room, setting, 30 → 31; then Apply.
slides.narration: Think of checking your online shopping basket before you pay. In this fictional paper example, the saved Rescue floor is thirty percent and the allowed step is one point. Thirty plus one step is thirty one. Type thirty one, or drag the line. The draft line moves to thirty one while the saved line stays at thirty. Now select Review changes. A review box opens and names the room the change affects. It lists the setting with its old value and new value: thirty, then an arrow, then thirty one. Read every row against what you meant to do. The button at the bottom says Apply one change. Apply is the only step that sends the value to Home Assistant, where the Controller reads its targets. In the isolated demo, Apply changes sample data only. If a row is wrong, select Back to editing instead. Next, you check that the change was accepted.

workedExample.prompt: What changes when a saved 30% Rescue floor becomes a 31% draft?
steps: Record the saved value, 30%, and the allowed step, 1 point.
Set the draft: 30 + 1 = 31%.
See the draft line move while the saved line stays at 30%.
Select Review changes and check room, setting, 30 → 31 before Apply.
workedExample.answer: Only the proposed Rescue floor changes. Recorded readings and the saved 30% stay until Apply and readback.

check.prompt: Review changes shows Rescue floor 30 → 32. You meant 31. What do you do?

options.text: Apply, then fix it later.
options.feedback: Fixing later means two changes and a wrong value in between. Correct the draft first.

options.text: Back to editing, fix the draft, review again.
options.feedback: Right. The review exists to catch exactly this.

options.text: Apply; one point does not matter.
options.feedback: One point on a safety level does matter. Apply only what you meant.

slides.title: Check the receipt, then restore
body: Readback: the value Home Assistant actually accepted.
Restore 31 → 30 by the same draft, review, apply, readback.
slides.narration: After you pay, you check the receipt. After Apply, you check the readback. Readback means the app reads the value back from Home Assistant and shows what was actually accepted. While it works, the button says Applying and verifying. If Home Assistant refused a value, the box says Some changes were not applied, and gives the reason. That value stays in your draft for review. If the result is unclear, for example because the connection dropped, find out what was accepted before you try again. When the readback shows thirty one, put things back. Restoring means returning to the starting value you wrote down. Thirty one minus one step is thirty. Use the same path: draft thirty, Review changes, Apply, then read back thirty. Practising the way back matters as much as the way forward. Next, try it in a different zone.

options.text: The change was refused; the target is still 30%.
options.feedback: Right. Read the reason before trying again.

options.text: The target is 31%; the message is cosmetic.
options.feedback: The readback is the receipt. It says 30%, so 31% was not accepted.

options.text: The target is now 0%.
options.feedback: A refusal never means zero. Read the value shown and the reason.

slides.title: Try another demo zone
body: Use that zone’s own start value and allowed step.
A zone value overrides the room value for that zone only.
slides.narration: A recipe that worked in one kitchen still needs checking in another. Choose a different zone, ideally in another demo room. Use its own starting value and its own allowed step, rather than copying thirty and thirty one. Before you edit, predict which line will move. Then make one step, review, apply, read back, restore, and read back again. One more idea matters here. The Zone list also has an option called Room lights and shared targets. A value set there applies to every zone in the room. A value set on one zone overrides the room value, for that zone only. Example: the room re-water threshold is sixty percent, and Zone three has its own value of fifty eight. Zone three uses fifty eight. Every other zone uses sixty. Check which scope you are editing before you apply. Next, recall the whole journey.

options.feedback: A zone value applies to that zone only. Zone 4 falls back to the room value.

options.text: 60%, the room value.
options.feedback: Right. With no value of its own, Zone 4 uses the room’s 60%.

options.text: No threshold at all.
options.feedback: A zone without its own value uses the room value.

slides.title: Recall the complete change journey
body: Draft → Review changes → Apply → Readback; restore the same way.
Armed schedule targets change in Calendar.
slides.narration: Teach the shopping journey to someone else without looking at the screen. The draft proposes a change in this browser. Review changes shows the room, the setting, the old value and the new value. Apply sends it to Home Assistant. Readback shows what was accepted. Restoring uses the same four steps to go back. Then name the lines. The saved reference shows the stored target. The draft shows your proposal. The dark solid lines show what the probes recorded. Finally, say who owns the targets. If Target source says armed schedule, a grow plan owns them, and you change them in Calendar. Check that the demo value is back where it started, and note both readback values in your practice record. A clean record shows the next person that nothing was left half changed. Next lesson, you build that grow plan in Calendar.

slides.narration: Halfway between two numbers sits in the middle. Shot size is how much water each P two shot gives, as a share of the substrate volume, as in B four. In this fictional profile, the P two shot size is two percent at the vegetative endpoint. At the generative endpoint it is four percent. The difference is four minus two, which is two. Half of two is one. Add one to two, and the halfway blend is three percent, before rounding to the setting’s step. The probe may rise by a different amount. Now give it dates. If Zone one starts on the first of March, day seven is the seventh of March. Assign the profile to days one to seven, then read the blocks either side. slides.title: Store first, then request activation
body: Review & save: checks and stores the plan, still as a draft.
Arm plan: start at the next local lights-on (activation).
Arming never turns Watering on or starts a pump.
slides.narration: Booking a flight, checking in and boarding are separate steps. A grow plan has the same kind of steps. First, Review and save. The app checks the draft for problems, then stores it in Home Assistant. A saved plan is still a draft. Second, Arm plan. Arming is a request: start using this plan at the next local lights-on. The Arm plan button stays unavailable until the Controller reports that it supports plans. Third, activation. Activation is the moment the Controller takes over the plan’s dated targets. Example: you arm at three in the afternoon, and lights-on is at six in the morning. From three in the afternoon to six the next morning is fifteen hours, so activation comes fifteen hours later. Check the status the Controller reports, not only your click. Fourth, and separate from all of these, is the Watering switch in the top bar. Arming never turns Watering on and never starts a pump. Next, learn how to hand control back.

slides.title: Understand the return handover
body: Disarm plan: manual targets return at the next lights-on.
Edit again only when the status reads draft.
Plan hold: no plan steering, but safety watering still runs.
slides.narration: A shift handover happens at a set time, not halfway through a task. Disarm plan asks the Controller to go back to manual targets at the next lights-on. Until then, the plan’s targets stay in force. Wait for the status to read draft before you edit. From then on, the plan is yours to change again. A plan hold is a different thing. A hold happens when a zone’s day in the plan is missing, finished or invalid. The Controller then stops steering that zone by the plan, rather than invent targets. Safety watering still runs during a hold, such as the overnight rescue shot below the Rescue floor. So a hold pauses the plan, and the zone can still get water. If water flows when it should not, use the physical shutdown at the equipment first. Disarm plan and a hold are software states, and they come after that. Next, practise a second block on your own.

slides.title: A budget and a statement answer different questions
body: Timeline: Controller records, newest first.
Water use: litres per zone. Compare runs: two runs side by side.
Grows: run records with names and dates.
slides.narration: A budget says what you planned to spend. A bank statement shows what was actually spent. The app has both kinds of information. Targets are the budget. History is the statement. Open History in the isolated demo. It has four main tabs. Timeline is one list of the Controller’s records, such as shots, phase changes and target changes, newest first. Water use shows the litres each zone was given today, this grow week and since the grow started. A run is one grow in one room, from start to finish. Compare runs puts the run in progress beside an earlier run, week by week. Grows holds the run records: the name, start date and end date of each run. Before you open any tab, write down your question, the room, the zone and the time period. For example: did Zone two in Room A get more water on day ten than last run? A clear question tells you which tab to open. Next, make sure two runs are fair to compare.

body: Match grow age, zone, plant count, units and EC type.
Coverage: how much of the period has records. Missing ≠ zero.
slides.narration: Comparing one child’s height at age five with another’s at age eight tells you little. You compare at the same age. Grow age is the number of days since a run started. Compare day ten with day ten. Next, match the zone. Check it had the same plant count and the same setup in both runs. Then match the units and the type of EC. Pore-water EC and feed EC are different measurements, as you learned in A five. Last, check coverage. Coverage means how much of the period actually has recorded data. In Compare runs, the section called Data quality and history coverage shows each day’s recorded range as a bar. Example: one run has twenty four hours of records for day ten, and the other has six hours. That is not a fair match. A day with no records stays empty, and empty is different from zero. Next, try a fair comparison.

A: 12 L estimated; B: 15 L estimated; 15 − 12 = 3 L.

slides.narration: Now a fair comparison. Two fictional runs have complete day ten records for the same zone, with the same plant count. Run A shows twelve litres of estimated delivery. Run B shows fifteen. Subtract twelve from fifteen. That is three. So Run B received three litres more estimated delivery on day ten. Remember from B four: delivery is water supplied through the drippers, runoff is water that drains out, and uptake is water that enters the plant. Water use counts delivery, worked out from each shot’s runtime and the configured dripper flow. Keep the word estimated in your sentence. Three litres more delivery does not show the plants took up three litres more, or that a target change caused it. Climate, plant size and other changes can all play a part. A careful sentence is: Run B shows three litres more estimated delivery on matched day ten. Next, date the reference you compare against.

slides.title: Date the reference as carefully as the reading
body: Target reference: what you compare readings against.
Snapshot: targets saved at one moment, with a time stamp.
A run recorded late gets today’s targets, not past ones.
slides.narration: A budget is only useful if you know which month it was written for. A target reference is the same. Here, a reference is the set of targets you compare the readings against. In Compare runs, open the full-resolution chart and select a Target reference. There are three choices: Current configured daily plan, Saved run daily reference, and Current phase reference. A snapshot is a copy saved at one moment, with a time stamp. When you save a run record in Grows, the app saves a snapshot of the targets at that moment. Example: today is the twentieth of October, and you record last month’s run for the first time. Its snapshot holds today’s targets, not last month’s. Targets nobody saved cannot be rebuilt. Read the note beside the reference. It says when the reference was captured and where it came from. Comparing old readings with the wrong month’s targets leads to false conclusions. Next, label the delivery figure correctly.

slides.title: Your turn: name what the estimate means
body: Runtime × configured flow = estimated delivery, not uptake.
Per plant = zone total ÷ plant count: an average.
slides.narration: A taxi meter estimates the fare from time and distance. Delivery figures work the same way. The app multiplies each shot’s runtime by the configured dripper flow. That gives estimated delivery. Measured delivery would need a water meter or a catch test. Complete the sentence in your head: runtime times flow estimates delivery, not plant what? Pause. The answer is uptake. A per-plant figure adds one more step. It divides the zone total by the plant count from setup. Example: twelve litres across six plants is twelve divided by six, which is two litres per plant on average. Some plants may have had more and some less, if a dripper was blocked. When you copy a number into a report, keep its label beside it: measured, estimated or unknown. A label lost in a report becomes a false fact for the next reader. Next, try a messy comparison.

slides.narration: Comparing one day’s shopping with a whole week’s would make the week look expensive. Here, one record covers day six only. The other covers days one to six. One run is also missing its pore-water EC readings. Are their totals comparable? Decide first. They are not, because the periods differ. Choose a matched period with good coverage, such as day six in both. Why might data be missing? Home Assistant stores past readings in a part called the Recorder. The Recorder keeps readings for a limited time, and that time is called retention. Older readings are removed. Water use can also read Home Assistant’s long-term statistics, which are kept with no time limit. A longer chart cannot bring back readings the Recorder removed. title: Troubleshoot before you change a recipe
summary: When something looks wrong, make it safe, keep the evidence, find the real cause and prove the repair, before touching any target.
outcomes: Use the physical shutdown first for water that will not stop.

slides.title: Repair the evidence before turning the dial
body: Make safe → preserve → investigate → verify.
Water that will not stop: physical shutdown first.
slides.narration: If a fridge thermometer’s battery dies, turning the thermostat colder does not fix the thermometer. A fault is anything that stops the system working as it should. Examples are a dead probe, a valve that will not close, or a wrong reading. A fault needs a repair, not a new target. Use the same four steps every time, in this order. One, make safe. If water keeps flowing when it should not, use the physical shutdown first. Remember from C one: the physical shutdown is the hand-operated way to cut water or power at the equipment itself. Two, preserve. Write down what you saw, with times, before anything changes. Three, investigate. Find the real cause with competent help, meaning someone trained on your site’s equipment. Four, verify. Prove the fix worked, with fresh readings and a look at the equipment. Example: a reading drops to zero at two o’clock. Changing a target would leave that reading broken. Next, work through an old reading.

body: Last reported 06:10; now 10:10: the reading is four hours old.

slides.narration: A note on the fridge saying the milk is fine means little if it was written last week. In this fictional example, a zone is holding. Holding means the Controller is giving it no shots for now. The zone’s moisture reading was last reported at six ten. It is now ten ten. From six ten to ten ten is four hours, so the reading is four hours old. Lowering a threshold would leave the old reading in place. Instead, follow the four steps. Make safe: nothing is flowing, so the zone is already safe. Preserve: record the room, the zone, the time and the reason shown in Why slash next action. Investigate: open Equipment, Probes. Read the probe’s health, such as Silent or Not reporting. Then, with competent help, check its cable, its power and its mapping, the link between the name on screen and the real probe. Verify: wait for fresh readings and a normal status before you think about targets again. Next, two readings that disagree.

slides.title: Conflicting tank evidence needs a real check
body: Tank display 80%; low float says low: conflicting evidence.
Keep protections on; look at the tank, then check each sensor.
slides.narration: If a car’s fuel gauge shows half full but the low fuel light is on, one of them is wrong. A tank level sensor measures how full the feed tank is. Some tanks also have a low float: a floating switch that reports low when the water drops past it. Here, the tank display says eighty percent, but the low float says low. That is conflicting evidence: two sources that cannot both be right. Averaging them would invent a level, and choosing eighty because it reassures you would hide the fault. Keep the protections switched on. When a tank level is mapped, the Controller holds shots at eight percent or less, or when the low float reads low. That hold stops the pump running a dry tank. Look at the tank itself, safely. Then check each sensor’s mapping, calibration and last report time. Record which check settled the disagreement. Next, a saved setup the Controller has not accepted.

options.feedback: An average of two conflicting sources is a number nobody measured.

options.text: Keep protections on and look at the tank itself.
options.feedback: Right. A direct look settles which source is wrong.

slides.title: A stored setup needs Controller acceptance
body: Saved: the new setup revision is stored.
Acknowledged: the Controller confirms the revision it accepted.
Commissioned: a supervised water test proves outlets run and stop.
slides.narration: Posting a letter, the letter arriving, and the reader acting on it are three different events. Setup changes have three similar stages. If you skipped the setup lessons, here they are in plain words. Equipment, Setup is where an administrator links each zone to its real valves and probes. That link is the mapping. Each saved version of the setup gets a number, called a revision. Stage one: Save configuration stores the new revision in Home Assistant. Stage two: acknowledgement. The Controller reports which revision it has accepted, like a signed receipt. Check that it matches, and that the heartbeat, the Controller’s regular report that it is running, is recent. Until the Controller accepts the revision, keep the room’s Watering switch off. Stage three: commissioning. Commissioning is a supervised test with real water. It proves each valve feeds the right drippers and then stops. Next, the most urgent case.

slides.title: Your turn: OFF displayed, water flowing
body: Off on screen, water flowing: physical shutdown first.
Then check for a sticking valve, siphon, wrong mapping, old timer.
slides.narration: A light switch in the off position with the bulb still glowing tells you the switch is not the whole story. The screen says off, but water is visibly flowing. Finish the first response aloud: physical shutdown. Close the water or cut the power at the equipment, using your site’s procedure. Then investigate with competent help. There are four common causes. A sticking valve is a valve that stays partly open after it is told to close. A siphon, which you met in C one, is water that keeps running downhill through the pipe on its own. A wrong mapping means the screen controls a different valve. An old timer or another system may still switch the same valve. Remember from C one: each output needs one owner. Stop all, Disarm plan and a plan hold are all software requests, so they come after the physical shutdown, not instead of it. Next, write a fault report.

slides.title: Try another fault report independently
body: Zone 2 shot, no rise; Zone 3 rose instead.
Report: room, zone, time, expected, actual, evidence.
slides.narration: A good doctor’s note says what happened and when, before guessing why. In this case, a shot ran for Zone two, but Zone two’s moisture did not rise. Zone three, next door, rose instead. Write the observation first: room, zone, event time, what you expected and what actually happened. Example: Room A, Zone two, shot at ten fifteen, expected a rise of about two points, saw none. Zone three rose two points at ten seventeen. Then list possible causes without choosing one. The valves may be mapped the wrong way round. The probes may be in the wrong pots. Delivery may have failed. Check the zone names, the times and the commissioning records. Arrange checks with competent help, rather than switching valves one after another to see what happens. Leave out passwords and access tokens, the digital keys that let software sign in. A clear report lets someone else find the cause quickly. Next, recall the sequence.

slides.title: Recall the repair sequence
body: Make safe → preserve → investigate → verify.

slides.narration: Teach the four steps to someone else without notes: make safe, preserve, investigate, verify. Then explain how repairing a sensor differs from changing a target. A repair fixes the information. A target change tells the Controller to aim somewhere else, using whatever information it has. Verifying means fresh readings and a normal status. It also means a look at the equipment in its agreed final state, such as valves closed. After a valve or mapping repair, a supervised commissioning test may be needed again. Ask your site’s responsible person what you do not yet know about the physical shutdown. Where is it? What does it switch off? Who may use it? Finish your record with the fault, the repair evidence and the name of the person doing the next check. Next lesson, you build a short daily routine.

title: A five-minute daily check and a useful handover
summary: Run a short preflight, keep a five-part diary, make one reasoned decision, treat the AI assistant as advice to check, and leave a handover the next person can use.
outcomes: Run a preflight and complete the five-part daily record.

slides.title: A short preflight, then a brief diary
body: Preflight: a quick check before you decide anything.
Five parts: identity, state, water, feed and context, decision.
slides.narration: Before take-off, a pilot walks round the plane with a checklist. That short check is called a preflight. After landing, the pilot writes a log. Use the same rhythm each day. First, a preflight: a quick look at the screens and the room before you decide anything. Then a daily diary: a short written record of what you found and what you decided. The diary has five parts. One, identity and freshness: which room and zone, and how old each reading is. Two, state: the phase and the reason. Three, water: how much was delivered. Four, feed and context: the tank, the EC and the room conditions. Five, the decision. About five minutes is a good routine on a normal day. A fault takes as long as it needs. If a source has no current reading, write unknown, as you learned in D one. Next, fill in the first four parts.

slides.narration: A weather report gives the place, the time, the conditions and the outlook, in that order. The first four diary parts work the same way. Identity and freshness: write the room, the zone, the time, the Controller’s report age from the top bar, and each probe’s report age. State: the phase, the reason from Why slash next action, the last shot, and any equipment state the screen confirms. Water: the delivery total, and if useful the per-plant average, each labelled measured, estimated or unknown, as in D four. Feed and context: the tank level, which type of EC you are reading, and anything unusual in the room, such as a hot afternoon. Example: Room A, Zone one, eight fifteen. Controller one minute, probe two minutes. P one. Eleven litres estimated. These four parts are the evidence. The fifth part, the decision, rests on them. Next, a decision to change nothing.

slides.narration: A health check-up that finds nothing wrong is still a useful check-up. In this fictional example, Training North, Zone three, has recent reports, the expected P two phase and a clear waiting reason. Today’s estimated delivery is fourteen litres. The last five days ranged from thirteen to fifteen litres, so fourteen sits inside the usual range. The tank level and the low float agree. The decision is no change. Write that decision down, with the reason and when you will check again. A decision record is the part of the diary that says what you decided, why, and when you will look again. For example: No change. Delivery within the usual thirteen to fifteen litres. Next check at two in the afternoon. Changing a target every day only to have done something adds noise and hides real problems. Next, record a change when one is needed.

slides.narration: A note on a recipe is only useful if it says what you changed and how it turned out. When a change is justified, the decision record needs more. Write the scope, meaning the room and zone. Write the before and after values. Write the reason, and what you expect to see next. Then make the change with the path from D two: draft, Review changes, Apply, then readback. Finish with a follow-up: a time when you will check the result. Example: Room A, Zone two. Rescue floor thirty to thirty one percent, as agreed with the head grower. Expect the Rescue floor line one point higher on the chart. Readback thirty one. Check tomorrow at seven. If you change two things on the same day, record both. A better day after two changes cannot tell you which one helped. Next, the AI assistant.

slides.title: Use the AI assistant as advice to check
body: Check its readings, report times, scope, units and assumptions.
Filled mark: action. Outline mark: advice, no action or refusal.

slides.narration: A sat nav can suggest a route, but you still watch the road. The app has an AI assistant. AI stands for artificial intelligence: software that writes answers in everyday language. Find it under Settings and help, AI assistant. Its decisions also appear as marks on the zone page chart. A filled mark is an action it took. An outline mark is advice, no action or a refusal. The AI assistant can organise a question or explain a proposal. It does not measure the crop. Check what its suggestion rests on: the readings, their report times, the room, the zone, the units and its assumptions. Example: it suggests a lower re-water threshold, but cites a probe reading that is three hours old. That suggestion rests on old evidence. Any change you accept still goes through review and readback. Keep passwords and access tokens out of your questions and screenshots. Next, prepare a handover.

body: Another zone, one source unknown: five parts and a decision.
Handover: who, versions, backup location, recovery, final state.

slides.narration: A good shift handover means the next person can carry on without phoning you. First, practise another day. Choose a different demo zone, and suppose one source has no current reading. Complete the five parts, then decide: keep the settings, investigate, or make one justified demo change. Say why. Then write a handover note: a short note that gives the next responsible person what they need. Include who is responsible now, the software versions, where the backup is, how to recover, and the agreed final state of the equipment. A backup is a saved copy of the whole setup that can be restored after a failure. A backup counts once someone has restored it successfully in a test. An update installs a newer software version. Rollback means going back to the previous version if an update causes trouble. Follow your site’s update and rollback guide. Next, teach it back.

Then show them the change path in the demo: draft, Review changes, Apply, readback and restore. Some skills cannot be learned from a screen. Where the physical shutdown is, and what commissioning proved at your site, need a competent local person to show you. Tomorrow, recall without notes the difference between a draft, Apply and Arm plan. In about a week, solve an old-reading case with new numbers. Spacing practice out like this makes it stick. Keep your diary short, specific and honest about anything still unresolved. That completes the daily operation lessons.

options.text: Change a target so the check has an outcome.
options.feedback: A useful check supports a decision; changing targets is not mandatory.

options.text: Record no change, its reason and the next check.
options.feedback: Correct. A reasoned no-change decision is a useful record.

options.text: Skip the record because nothing changed.
options.feedback: Evidence and follow-up still help the next operator understand the day.

quiz.prompt: The AI assistant recommends a target. How should you handle it?

options.text: Trust its confident explanation.
options.feedback: Fluent advice does not check readings, crop response or what Home Assistant accepted.

options.text: Treat a chart mark as proof.
options.feedback: A mark records an event. It does not prove the advice is sound.

options.text: Check its evidence and assumptions; review and read back any change you accept.
options.feedback: Correct. Advice, accepted changes and physical results are separate evidence.

quiz.prompt: Which record best supports a review?

options.text: Scope, before/after, reason, context, readback and follow-up.
options.feedback: Correct. These let another operator assess intent and outcome.

options.text: Better recipe, applied today.
options.feedback: This omits values, scope, evidence, acceptance and a check time.

options.text: One improved day proves success.
options.feedback: One day cannot isolate cause; other changes and conditions may explain it.

quiz.prompt: What must precede independent operation of the physical system?

options.text: Online quizzes alone.
options.feedback: Online knowledge cannot establish safe mapping, physical stopping or local competence.

options.text: Competent local handover and verified commissioning evidence.
options.feedback: Correct. Identify shutdown, output owners, records and safe procedures with local supervision.

options.text: An AI summary saying it is safe.
options.feedback: AI advice cannot replace physical commissioning or a competent handover.

instructions: Complete the daily record and teach scope to another learner in the demo.
With competent local supervision, review physical shutdown, commissioning evidence, backups and recovery roles.
Record missing handover items as unresolved; do not claim physical competence from this lesson.
